questions.problem:
$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x(t))+y(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)=1-{x}^{2}(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }0]^{T}?$

$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y \\ 1-{x}^{2}\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+y)=1 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(1-{x}^{2})=-2x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(1-{x}^{2})=0\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & 1 \\ -2x & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi (1)) & 1 \\ -2(1) & 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 1 \\ -2 & 0\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}-1-\lambda  & 1 \\ -2 & -\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ -\lambda \cdot (-1-\lambda )-1\cdot (-2) & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}+\lambda +2 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=-\frac{1}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{7}}{2}\text{i}.$

Finally, since we have two complex eigenvalues with negative real parts, our equilibrium is an $\text{asymptotically stable}$ $\text{spiral sink}.$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x(t))+{y}^{2}(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)y(t)\end{aligned}
$$

Given the system of differential equations, select the correct options below.

The Jacobian determinant of the system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}$ is given as

$$
J(0,0)={{field-1}}.
$$

At this point, the system is 
{{field-2}}

questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+{y}^{2} \\ {x}^{2}y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian determinant of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}|
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+{y}^{2})=\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x),\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi x)+{y}^{2})=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}y)=2xy,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}y)={x}^{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
J=|\begin{aligned}\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi x) & 2y \\ 2xy & {x}^{2}\end{aligned}|.
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\begin{aligned}J(0,0) & =|\begin{aligned}\pi \operatorname{cos}⁡(0) & 2(0) \\ 2(0)(0) & {0}^{2}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\pi  & 0 \\ 0 & 0\end{aligned}| \\  & =\pi \cdot 0-0\cdot 0 \\  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, since the Jacobian determinant is zero, our system is $\text{not almost linear}$ at ${x}^{∗}.$

questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={y}^{2}(t)-x(t) \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+2y(t)\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[0,\text{ }0]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{y}^{2}-x \\ {x}^{2}+2y\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({y}^{2}-x)=-1,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({y}^{2}-x)=2y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+2y)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+2y)=2\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2y \\ 2x & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 2(0) \\ 2(0) & 2\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}-1 & 0 \\ 0 & 2\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}0 \\ 0\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}].
$$

questions.problem:
$$ \{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)+4y(t)-2x(t)-3 \\ {y}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}(t)-{y}^{2}(t)+3y(t)-3\end{aligned} $$ Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the corresponding linearized system at the equilibrium point ${x}^{∗}=[1,\text{ }1]^{T}?$
${u}^{′}=\,\,$ {{field-1}} {{field-2}} $\,\,u,\,$ where $u=x-{x}^{∗}$
{{field-3}} {{field-4}}
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+4y-2x-3 \\ {x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3y-3\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+4y-2x-3)=2x-2,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+4y-2x-3)=4 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3y-3)=2x,\, & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}-{y}^{2}+3y-3)=-2y+3\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x-2 & 4 \\ 2x & -2y+3\end{aligned}].
$$

Next, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(1)-2 & 4 \\ 2(1) & -2(1)+3\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}].
$$

Finally, near the equilibrium, the nonlinear system is approximated by

$$
{u}^{′}=[\begin{aligned}0 & 4 \\ 2 & 1\end{aligned}]u,
$$

where the deviation vector is

$$
u=x-{x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]-[\begin{aligned}1 \\ 1\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}x-1 \\ y-1\end{aligned}].
$$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}{x}^{′}(t)={x}^{2}+xy-6 \\ {y}^{′}(t)=-{y}^{2}+2x-3\end{aligned}
$$

Consider the system of differential equations above. What is the behavior of the system's solutions near the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}={[2,\text{ }1]}^{T}?$

$\,$
The equilibrium is an 
{{field-1}}{{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
The system can be rewritten in matrix form as 

$$
{x}^{′}=\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)
$$

where $x=[\begin{aligned}x(t) \\ y(t)\end{aligned}]$ and 
$\text{\boldsymbol}f(x)=[\begin{aligned}{x}^{2}+xy-6 \\ -{y}^{2}+2x-3\end{aligned}].$

We need to compute the Jacobian matrix (or the total derivative) of $\text{\boldsymbol}f(x).$ 

In our case, we have the following:

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y}\end{aligned}]
$$

First, we compute the partial derivatives:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}({x}^{2}+xy-6)=2x+y \\ \frac{∂{f}_{1}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}({x}^{2}+xy-6)=x \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂x} & =\frac{∂}{∂x}(-{y}^{2}+2x-3)=2 \\ \frac{∂{f}_{2}}{∂y} & =\frac{∂}{∂y}(-{y}^{2}+2x-3)=-2y\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}(x)=[\begin{aligned}2x+y & x \\ 2 & -2y\end{aligned}].
$$

Now, we evaluate the Jacobian at the equilibrium ${x}^{∗}=[\begin{aligned}2 \\ 1\end{aligned}]$ to get

$$
\text{\boldsymbol}{f}^{′}({x}^{∗})=[\begin{aligned}2(2)+1 & 2 \\ 2 & -2(1)\end{aligned}]=[\begin{aligned}5 & 2 \\ 2 & -2\end{aligned}].
$$

Notice that the matrix is invertible (its determinant is not zero), so the system is almost linear at ${x}^{∗}.$

To find the eigenvalues of the Jacobian matrix, we write down the characteristic equation:

$$
\begin{aligned}|\begin{aligned}5-\lambda  & 2 \\ 2 & -2-\lambda \end{aligned}| & =0 \\ (5-\lambda )(-2-\lambda )-4 & =0 \\ {\lambda }^{2}-3\lambda -6 & =0\end{aligned}
$$

Solving the equation, we get the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1,2}=\frac{3}{2}\pm \frac{\sqrt{33}}{2}.$

Since the eigenvalues are real and have opposite signs, our equilibrium is an $\text{unstable}$ $\text{saddle}.$
